utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I've just been asked to put on the record, Your Honours, that the document which was the subject of your ruling at the end of the proceedings yesterday afternoon, earlier in the day received Exhibit Number D2817 when it was used by Dr. Karadzic with General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that I have very little time, I wanted to join a couple of topics. You told us why the troops were persistent and brave because they were a people's army defending their homes. Were there any negative consequences for the security of officers because it was not a professional army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D7534.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, General? Somebody signed it for you, but your name is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is it about briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist is that an order is being issued specifying measures to protect officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reasoning behind it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was wilful conduct by individuals and people reacted inappropriately concerning some commands that were issued to them and a number of officers found themselves in danger due to the behaviour of certain groups of -- or irresponsible people. As far as I know, it even went as far as one commander, brigade commander, being killed. He was not from the SRK. In that regard, measures and orders were issued in order to improve the security of officers and the way the military police was used to provide security for those officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the area of your corps, were there any murders, especially of civilian dignitaries by our soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. In Grbavica, the president of the Executive Council of Novo Sarajevo municipality was killed, Budo Obradovic. Before holding that position, he had been a battalion commander as part of the 1st Romanija Brigade. He was the epitome of someone who went about his work fairly and appropriately. The civilian and military police investigated his case. I am not aware of any details. I just know that the man was killed. I don't know to what extent it was documented in terms of procedure. As for Colonel Jovo Bartula, who commanded the artillery regiment in the SRK, was wounded due to the wilful conduct of some people. He had been wounded in his arm. So the consequences were not as serious, but still it was a reflection of that type of behaviour vis-a-vis officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2842, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I have to move to the next topic immediately to discuss the relationship between the president of the republic and the commander of the Main Staff. In the briefest of terms, can you tell us what you knew about it and what was your view of that relationship?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My screen doesn't seem to be working, so I won't be waiting for any documents. I have a specific opinion, position, regarding that, although its importance was far broader than what I will try to explain here, trying to put my answers within the time allotted. My knowledge or my estimate that I reached based on what was going on between the President of Republika Srpska and the commander of the Main Staff is that the relationship was detrimental. It was not a good one. The person who did not work on improving that relationship was Mr. Mladic. He wanted to be dominant in all situations without respecting the structure, level of address, and the people's positions in our area. That is to say, in the area of Republika Srpska. I was quite displeased. There were a number of situations which indicated that things were wrong. I never had occasion at any meeting or encounter to hear from the horse's mouth, so to say, what the root of the problem was in your relationship with Mr. Mladic. I don't know whether it was a matter of argument or open confrontation. I simply know that Mladic refused having anyone on a higher position than his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you remember that in early August 1995, I attempted to change the structure and establishment formation in order to change the Main Staff into a General Staff and make certain personnel changes? It was in document D2159. If you recall, all of the generals at the time save for yourself supported Mladic. D2159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's very leading, Mr. Karadzic. You're not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to draw the attention of the participants to the following, and I would like to ask the General the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the generals in this attempt of mine concerning General Mladic, and what was your position? Why were you not on the same side or list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? The question you put, in order for me to be able to explain to the Chamber, it requires a somewhat long explanation. However, I will do my best to bring it down to only a few sentences. It is all true. There was an attempt following the president's decision to have Mr. Mladic removed. It's a well-known matter. What followed was his objection or refusal. He did so by gathering the generals, rallying the generals against the measure. It indeed took place. We all know what the dates in question are. Some were in early August. All of the generals arrived in Banja Luka, and it was very clear that they accepted General Mladic's position in the sense that the president of the republic was wrong and that Mladic should not be removed. I was not in Banja Luka at that moment when the gathering took place since I was still engaged in combat. I have to repeat once again all areas were important to me, especially the situation in the Nisici plateau. As I was there, no one managed to communicate with me to tell me that I was expected to appear anywhere, be it with Mladic or President Karadzic given the fact that both sides had summoned the generals. I was completely unaware of it. When I returned to the command, my associates briefed me on what went on. That same afternoon, I set off together with Colonel Cedo Sladoje. We wanted to see President Karadzic in an attempt to help resolve the situation or even things out so as to perhaps gain a better insight as to whether the removal should take place or not. We visited Mr. Karadzic, and he wasn't able to make a decision at the time. The very next day I went to Banja Luka to find General Mladic. I wanted the whole thing to be resolved in a more intelligent way, but it was also my estimate that I was not the kind of mediator who could even things out. I found Mladic not in Banja Luka, but I was transported by helicopter to Ostrelj. It's a hill, a mountain, just outside Drvar. I found him there. He explained it to me and he told me what the other generals had accepted the day earlier. Then Croatian MiGs 21 and 29 arrived as part of their sources and there was a real threat that we would be killed at Ostrelj. That is why our conversation was very brief. It was my decision to accept his position as he persisted that he should not be removed. This is in the briefest possible terms, but actually that is how things developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it seen as you joining the other generals in supporting Mladic? Was that how the Main Staff saw it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how they interpreted my behaviour. That very day I was supposed to undergo an eye surgery at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. It was a very important health issue for me, but I asked for it to be postponed, and I left the next day from Banja Luka. I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the general public informed, as you recall, the Assembly and the general public were informed that the last of the generals had signed the last of the ones to be -- to give his opinion had signed in favour of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters were not able to hear your answer because you overlapped with the translation of Mr. Karadzic's question. If you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand. The general public was informed that I, too, had accepted the standpoint and joined the viewpoint of the other generals, and the conclusion was that I was supporting Mladic's conduct and attitude, although this was done, as I have said, it was not my intention to be the one, but it is true that it was used for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 8415.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a poor version. I have a better version in Serbian. This is a telegram. I have -- well, I'll read it to you. "To the Republika Srpska National Assembly, to the president of the Republika Srpska. "Dear sir, today the commander of the VRS Main Staff Colonel Mladic met the commander of the VRS Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Major-General Dragomir Milosevic who was informed of the content of the discussions at the expanded session of the advisory board. General Milosevic, like every other general of the Republika Srpska, was in entire agreement with all the decisions and conclusions adopted at the session including the letter addressed to the Republika Srpska National Assembly and the President of Republika Srpska regarding the decision of the president to relieve the commander of the VRS of duty and to order changes to the system, organisation, and staffing the VRS. Since Major-Generals Budimir Galic and Radivoje Miletic have previously expressed their support by telephone, it has been established that all the generals are absolutely united." Is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- is this what it says here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I confirm that this is what was announced, what was broadcast, but I heard that this was the case. I didn't know what the communique was, because I wasn't there. I was outside the area where this was taking place. I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the more legible version is on the other side of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2843, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us very briefly what the result was of this attempt of mine?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the result is well known. As I see it, there was no replacement of Mladic. There was no shake-up. I did not follow the situation further, so I can't say what its effects were or its impact on relations within the Army of Republika Srpska and the government organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at 65 ter 13935. This is a letter dated the 27th of August, 1995. Can we have -- well, this was signed by Miletic, not Jelacic, but the content is the same. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this decision of mine on my withdrawing my previous decisions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that the course of events was as described here, but as I have said, I did not receive information in writing. I did not see documents of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But were you aware that I myself had withdrawn my previous decrees?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I can't go through all the areas, but there's one topic I want to ask you about. What was the policy of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps vis-a-vis humanitarian aid passing through and arriving in Sarajevo? I'm speaking in general terms of humanitarian aid, utilities, electricity, water, and so on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say now that this is a highly complex issue linked to events throughout this period and the course of the war, that is, the conflict that obtained in the area I was in. It deserved a great deal of attention and the absolute care of everyone involved, both military and civilians. An area such as the area of Sarajevo, that's what I'm referring to now because I don't have all the information concerning humanitarian aid in Republika Srpska as a whole, the city of Sarajevo had to receive all kinds of humanitarian aid and everything that related to the population. I confirm that the flow and the activities were not disturbed by the command of the corps and were not obstructed in any way whatsoever, but I understood that the delivery had to be done in such a way that we would have to reassure ourselves as to what kind of goods were being sent. So everything that referred to attempts to smuggle in arms, ammunition, and other such things in these kinds of transports had to be efficiently established, and we had to make sure that this could not happen. So whenever such a thing did happen, that along with humanitarian aid a convoy would contain things that were prohibited, then that was a situation we had to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, what was the proportion of such instances in relation to the total number of convoys daily? How often did these problems arise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, but very often something would happen that was not in line with what had been agreed. However, in spite of this, it was my impression that humanitarian aid was not compromised, that it was not obstructed when one had to determine whether it had arrived in Sarajevo or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From whom -- by whom were you informed that the convoys had been approved and what was the further procedure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received that from the Main Staff. It all went through Mr. Indjic, and he passed on all this information to the organs in the command who were supposed to provide this information to the check-points controlling the entrance of convoys, and they would be told who was coming, what was coming, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see 1D7543, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is your document from 1993 in which you say that you had been informed by the Main Staff that they had approved this. Can you look at your instructions, the instructions you issued to your units concerning this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "To carry out reception, planned control, and secure movement along approved roads throughout. Firmly adhere to current rules and guidelines regarding movement of UNPROFOR convoys." I don't see the document any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this an exception? What was your attitude to this? What is this in fact? Is this a one-off situation, or did this kind of thing happen all the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Of course, we had to carry out certain checks and to have indicators. That was our regular practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know or were you able to know that this humanitarian aid being sent through to the civilian population under Muslim control, that it was also given to the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's another leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, what was the situation as regards food for your men in the corps? How did the supplies arrive in this period? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I remember. There was a shortage of foodstuffs, and this included both staples, strategic foodstuffs and those that were less important. That was a constant problem, and we had to seek a way to compensate for these shortages and to make sure that soldiers received the food that it was possible for them to receive, but these things came as humanitarian aid, and no one dared approve its use for the army. But speaking on my own behalf exclusively, I think that this practice was not all right because a soldier is also a human being and needs to eat and needs to be helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I told you that you would have half an hour today and the time's up. I'd like -- would like you to conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I thought that only my cross-examinations were to be limited and that when it comes to examination-in-chief I can schedule my time according to how -- how important I believe the witness to be, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber rarely limits your examination-in-chief. However, your estimate was only six hours for this witness, and you have spent almost 14 hours, and you indicated that your examination will have been concluded by yesterday. So I think it's more than reasonable to expect you to conclude in half an hour today. In any event, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D7545. I apologise -- well, I am sorry, Your Excellency, that I have to limit my witness to yes or no answers because he has much to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this document of yours from August 1993 and tell us briefly that you are drawing attention to the shortages in relation to your troops.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents speak of the problem and its size. For me, the problem was how to organise food for my soldiers. My soldiers were worried. They didn't know whether they had support and equipment for fighting. They were not so much concerned with the food, but I was the one who had to raise that issue with certain bodies in order to make sure that my troops had the necessary food.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, perhaps you can answer with yes or no. What was your attitude towards repairs of the water supply system and the electricity supply system that was needed to supply the other side, the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not be happy if you want me to answer by just yes or no since I know what was done in order to repair the water and electricity lines. We respected all requests by UNPROFOR, and we reacted to any need, and we did whatever was necessary to make sure that there was water, electricity, and all the other bare necessities for everybody. I personally, at the request of the CEO of Unioninvest, Mr. Bogdan Ceko, I made sure that the Moscanica water source was repaired, that people who were engaged in the repair works were protected. That water well supplied the city of Sarajevo. To be more precise, the old part of the city, and the repair works were done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D7544. Take a glance. This is your document [Realtime transcript read in error "indictment"]. Tell us whether this is the document that you have just described for us. 7544.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the document. This is my order whereby I ordered that the work of those men should be secure, that they should not be touched while engaged in the repair works.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission? Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what about the supply with electricity of our part of Sarajevo as opposed to the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one and the same. When there was no electricity in our part, there was no electricity over there and vice versa. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 1D7547.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the third paragraph from the bottom, where it says since electricity is necessary, you propose that a ring should be set up.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Later on people, and I mean repairsmen, did a fantastic job. There was constant fighting going on. Still they managed to connect the line and provide both sides with electricity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? And I have another document, and I will bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D7546. General, can you explain why you issued this proposal regarding alternative routes for convoys? Do you remember this document? Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Signature, yes. Let me see. Of course I remember. As a matter of fact, I see now what the document was about. My position was -- or better say, the position of the corps command was that no obstacles should be placed in the way of convoys. We wanted them to pass through as quickly as possible. That's why we proposed certain points through which movements should go, and that proposal implied guarantees for the bridges in the city, guarantees that there would be no disturbance on our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at bullet point 4 where you mention the reasons. You don't have to read. Just tell us what prompted you to issue this proposal.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was prompted with what you can read here. You can see what we did, what the -- kind of movements there were, what shortcomings may arise. When something could be spotted in our zone of responsibility, then a proper attitude could have been adopted to the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? And the last question. Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about any exact numbers, but just approximately, can you tell us how many sorties there were and how many landings at the Sarajevo airport daily? I'm talking about humanitarian aid, UNPROFOR flights, over the period of 1.300 days, and how big was the percentage of flights and landings that experienced problems on -- problems coming from any of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that I cannot give you anything that would be conclusive information. However, I can share with you my impression. You have to bear in mind that the corps command was very close to the airport and that we had a visual contact, and we did not have to rely on any information. We could see with our own eyes that the arrivals of certain aircraft at Sarajevo airport was to a large extent uneventful. It seems to me that that airport functioned even better than the airport here in Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you have all of these documents at your disposal during your trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. My trial and the intentions and the attempts or desires of my lawyer who wanted to achieve things and put in place some kind of defence system, it was not represented either partially or fully.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have no more time. I have questions but no time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I want to tell you that the situation regarding your trial is not relevant in this case, because we are not having a retrial or the judgement was -- your judgement was not in evidence in our case. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was on my feet to raise an objection as to the relevance of that line of -- that question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, will you not be taking into account for credibility purposes the fact that the witness has been convicted and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We also -- we take some judicial notice of some adjudicated facts from his case regarding convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but in light of that, don't you think that his explanation as to his trial is relevant if you're going to consider the fact that he's been convicted in terms of his credibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave it there at that time. Yes. Your examination-in-chief is over, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Just a quick transcript correction. At page 14, line 21, the question was put to the

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: your document." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecution, in particular Ms. Edgerton, representative of the Office the Prosecutor, but given the circumstances, in particular for her preparation, before we start hearing your cross-examination we -- we decided to hear three witnesses' evidence. So probably in my estimate you'll start being cross-examined tomorrow or Monday next week. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I would be grateful to you if I were given a short break. I don't know whether I may be allowed to tell you this. I have just one shirt. I don't have the time to deal with that and make myself presentable given the intensity of the way we work here. So if my cross-examination may be delayed until Monday, it would help me enormously to be able to cope with the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably that may be possible, but at the same time, the -- the Chamber does not want to lose its court -- courtroom time, so we'll see how it evolves. But before doing so, I have some questions about what you said with respect to Mr. Karadzic's attempt to remove Mr. Mladic from the position of his -- of the command of the VRS. You explained in detail what -- what you did or how you reacted to that -- in that regard, but could you tell us the reason for Mr. Karadzic to try to -- or attempt to remove him, and what's the point of disagreement with the civilian leadership and military leadership, and what was the rationale for the VRS generals to decide to support the -- Mladic's position? In other words, what was wrong with Mr. Karadzic? I was asking a compound question, but I believe that you will be capable of answering all the points.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll do my best to provide the answer based on my perception of the situation. I'm not purporting to say that I was on top of the situation and that I was aware of the deeper reasons for which Mr. Karadzic wanted to remove General Mladic. I can't tell you what exactly was the pretext, but I can share with you my impression, as I've already explained. We already started feeling -- or, rather, sensing that there were problems in relations between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. The relationship as it was, was the one of domination -- or, rather, Mladic wanted to be independent and not controlled by any superior body, and that was the structure of their overall relationship. I believe that that was the true indicator showing that he wanted to reap rewards of his popularity among people and achieve certain effects, perhaps in some future elections or something. I really can't say. I can only speculate. Your Honours, it seems to me yesterday on the screen there was a document which General Mladic issued in order to warn the corps command or, more precisely, he warns myself that I should not be doing certain things in relation to a meeting with civilian structures. That document was not actually addressed at me. There was a tendency to create an impression that civilian bodies were exercising certain things that were not in line with rules of combat. I don't have any evidence to support that, but I am saying that this was my feeling, that this is what the intention was. But I would like to say that this was not only the result of Mr. Mladic but also of those who were creating an atmosphere of a bad relationship between Mladic and Karadzic. Fuel was added to that fire from wider sources. I know that Mr. Mladic was bothered by my conduct, because I was not prepared to tell him, "General, sir, God has sent you to be our commander." The truth is, however, that I respected his orders, but I did not do it overzealously. I was not overzealous in my dealings with him, and that's why I was put under a lot of pressure. It was implied that I obeyed Mr. Karadzic, that I obeyed his orders. First of all, this is not correct. I never received any instructions or orders that would be issued for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps exclusively. Whatever arrived from the Presidency applied across the board to the Army of Republika Srpska and the developments surrounding the army. I was exposed to a lot of trouble. First of all, there were a lot of inaccuracies in the interpretation of my conduct and -- and falsities. First of all, I was perceived as being a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was never a member of any party by the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. There is no doubt about that. I was. I was mocked by some of the people from the Main Staff. For example, when they saw my jeep, my military vehicle, they would say, "There he is in the SDS jeep." That was a nonsense that could only insult me. I had to ignore all that and focus on those issues that we have discussed over the past few days. My main task was to look after the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its destiny. Certainly this may not be the most precise of answers. I'm sorry I had to be somewhat more expansive in my answer. When General Mladic entered my office at the corps command, he inspected my walls to see whether his photo was hanging on them, but he was also happy that President Karadzic's photo was not on the wall. The photo that I had on the wall was of Duke Misic, the famous hero from our past. As for the rest, we had to co-operate, and we were not supposed to allow ourselves to create the situation that existed during the Second World War where we had two sides, Chetniks on one side, Partisans on the other, and all that had disastrous consequences. That was my main concern, and I could not change anybody's attitude. I could only appeal to my former colleagues to change their attitude. Your Honours, I have nothing further to say in that respect. If you have any more questions, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You told me that General Mladic was sort of dominant and wanted to be independent from his superior. Does it mean that he was disobedient or defiant to -- to his commander, i.e., Supreme Commander? Do you have some examples where Mr. Mladic disobeyed the order from the president?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness receive appropriate interpretation of the word "defiant."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even see that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Disobedient or defiant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I said so. Now do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I understood it just the way you put it. That was the nature of his conduct. I cannot confirm, though, specifically where and when he may have put forth any requests or whatever one would call it inside civilian structures instead of orders. I can't say which ones he ignored or declined. I don't know that. Any details about the conflict between the two people is something I am not aware of. I don't have clear indications. I'm merely discussing my general impression, and that is the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And on your own you said the generals decided to support General Mladic and that Mr. Karadzic was wrong at the time. What was the reason for the conclusion that Mr. Karadzic had been wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I said that Dr. Karadzic was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'll read out what you said. It's transcript page 5, lines 9. "All of the generals arrived in Banja Luka, and it was very clear that they accepted General Mladic's position in the sense that the president of the republic was wrong and that Mladic should not be removed." Could you tell us the reason for such conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said. At the meeting they supported him. They supported Mladic. That means that they believed Karadzic was wrong. That piece of information that it was their estimate that Karadzic was wrong is not something as -- that I can use as any proof or source of knowledge. This is simply my understanding. If all of them arrived there and in their conversations with him they expressed their views that they support Mladic, this in turn meant that they were trying to say that Mr. Karadzic was wrong. That is the conclusion that one draws from it. I'm not asserting that they stated it in so many words, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then given the court schedule and in addition to the wish of the witness, it seems possible that we start the cross-examination of Mr. Milosevic on Monday. And in -- how much do you expect your cross-examination to last, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Preliminarily because I haven't had, obviously, the chance to digest the information this morning, I would say now, seven hours. On reflection, I might be able to reduce that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That adds more reason to defer the cross-examination to Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, when we have lost the habit that if we -- for the long weekends, why it shouldn't be Tuesday as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember, but the Chamber has some meetings, something like that. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But usually if we start Monday next week, we start Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic. We're out of synchronisation, though. This week is unusual. We normally would have sat -- not sat last Monday and sat on Friday, but for this week only it was changed, and therefore the knock-on effect is that we sit next Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we are going to take different regime in April and May. I think that has been informed. Mr. Milosevic, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear your cross-examination on Monday next week. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No translation. I don't think he got translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you hear my explanation that your examination -- cross-examination will start on Monday next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, Your Honour. I heard and understood. Everything's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Before we proceed, Mr. Robinson, the Chamber is -- is seized of the Defence filing of yesterday, i.e., the request for presence of counsel for Witness Edin Garaplija. I wonder whether you are in the position to answer why Mr. Garaplija is wanting a lawyer to be present during the testimony and what the legal basis for that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've been in touch with Mr. Garaplija's lawyer, and although I haven't put that exact question to him, I believe that the reason that Mr. Garaplija wants him to be present is because Mr. Garaplija was prosecuted for the events in which he is going to give evidence, and I think that there's some concerns concerning his rights about self-incrimination. And I'm not a hundred per cent sure what self-incrimination actually would exist since his case has been finished, but there's enough of a connection between his criminal case and his testimony that I think it would be fair for him to be represented by a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wasn't aware of his earlier conviction. Mr. Tieger, do you confirm that? Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He -- indeed, he was tried and convicted in Bosnia for -- I hesitate to speak unless I'm precisely sure of how -- the wording of the charges but I'm not at this moment, but indeed that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Prosecution does not object to the presence of his attorney to be present?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, would it be possible for me to read a very brief stipulation or agreement that the parties had reached concerning the evidence of Congressman Tony Hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed informally of that, but the Chamber would prefer to have it in writing by a joint -- joint submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hrsum. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, Mr. Hrsum, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt or could -- or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you believe that your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way will not be used as evidence in other cases against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hrsum.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and remind myself, because despite of my quite extensive experience here, I often forget, and that is that we have to pause between questions and answers so that the interpreters would be able to interpret it all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen before you, when the cursor stops moving and the letter A appears, it should be a prompt for you to start answering. That's better than losing something for the transcript. Mr. Hrsum, did you provide a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D7053 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the statement before you, Mr. Hrsum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us pause, please. Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you in this courtroom today that you were put by the Defence team, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I seek to tender this exhibit. It is under Rule 92 ter with an associated document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are requesting for a leave to -- to add to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are. We didn't have this document at the time we filed our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll grant the request and admit both of the documents. Shall we give the exhibit number for the statement first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit Number D2850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter 1D14001 will be Exhibit D2851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd now like to read out a summary in the English language of Mr. Hrsum's testimony. [In English] Tomislav Hrsum was born on 10th of June, 1957, in Rusanovici village, Rogatica municipality. He completed the secondary School of Internal Affairs in Sarajevo, after which he was assigned to Traffic Police Station 1 in Sarajevo. In the mid-1980s, he was appointed police inspector at the Sarajevo city S-U-P, SUP. From 1987, Tomislav Hrsum was assigned to the criminal investigation service at the Pale SJB station. Early in 1994, he was appointed chief of the criminal investigation service at the Pale SJB, where he stayed until the end of 1996. After that, he was assigned to the office of the RS MUP as the chief inspector. Right up until the outbreak of the war, the Pale SJB was a territorial and organisational unit of the Sarajevo city SUP, while functionally it was also linked to the Sarajevo security services centre whose purview was greater than that of the Sarajevo city SUP. The Pale SJB was financed and obtained all other materiel and technical equipment from the Sarajevo city SUP. The SDS established in July 1990 following the establishment of the SDA and HDZ. The SDS programme was equally -- equality of all nations and nationalities and resolving state matters through agreements. The SDS and the SDA had divided power in Pale and an agreement between the parties was formed. However, the SDA did everything in its power to ensure its predominance over the security organs. The SDA establishment of the Patriotic League in 1991 and the Green Berets caused fear and anxiety among the Serbs due to the partial inclusion in the police of these organisations. The Serbs did not have paramilitary formations as they supported and trusted the JNA to protect them. The Muslims refused to discharge their compulsory military service, meaning that the JNA comprised a high number of Serbs. Before the war, Muslims in Pale illegally procured weapons. At this time, the Assembly adopted a declaration of independence against the will of the Serbian people, and the Serbian deputies replied by forming an Assembly of the Serbian people in BH. Tomislav Hrsum is aware that at the beginning of 1992, members of the Sarajevo Stari Grad police station, with members of the Patriotic League, set up permanent check-points around Sarajevo. People from Pale were frequently abused at these check-points, their property and documents were seized, and this was often done by criminals who were members of the reserve police force and the Green Berets. Following this, all Serbian policemen in the Sarajevo Stari Grad SJB were expelled and disarmed which caused additional fear, uncertainty, and anxiety amongst the Serbs -- Serbian people. When a member of -- of a Serbian wedding party was killed in Bascarsija, Serbs gathered in Pale and relied on the police to make -- relied on the police to make sure -- to take measure and patrols were set up. In March 1992, Muslim policemen from the Pale area stated that they did not want to continue attending work and handed in their badges and weapons. However, some did not return these. Muslim paramilitary units blocked Pale municipality from all sides and attacked a Serbian settlement. A general mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, the armed forces for the RS, was only mobilised after the killing of JNA soldiers in Sarajevo. During the fighting, a large number of refugees from Sarajevo moved to Pale. A holding centre was established in the local gym whilst accommodation was found. Pale hosted approximately 400 Muslims who were being transferred to Central Bosnia. Accommodation was found in the gym for them and a guard was kept by JNA soldiers. Muslims in Pale were safe and went on with their regular activities and many people still had faith in the J -- SJB. However, when war broke out, members of paramilitary forces placed obstacles on the road disrupting traffic and abusing Serbs who were leaving the area. Muslims requested to leave Pale -- requests to leave Pale were granted in June 1992, and there were no incidents during this departure. Records were kept of these applications. When war broke out -- out all contacts with the Sarajevo city SUP and others ceased, and the jurisdiction were lost so that the functioning of the SJB, particularly in criminal investigation service, became blocked. Muslim paramilitary units blocked the territory of Pale on 6th of April, 1992, and there was immediately a problem in the form of a shortage of materiel and technical equipment required for work, and there was no way to implement the detention of persons. Muslim attacks continued. One incident occurred when approximately 50 soldiers were killed transporting food even after their passage had been agreed. Another attack took place on the day of a funeral for a JNA soldier. Muslims attacked Serbian positions while the soldiers were present at the funeral. Muslims also killed children, women, and elderly residents of Serbian villages and shelled the -- the war hospital in Koran causing considerable damage. In general, there were no paramilitary units in Pale area. However, there was one recorded incident with Arkan's Tigers who looted shops and removed vehicles. However, there were number of Muslim criminals in the area. Military security organs frequently submitted information about constant armed provocations, attacks and incursions in -- in the military facility of Renovica, which was armed -- from which armed inhabitants were removing and stealing weapons and military equipment. As a result, SJB police launched an operation to disarm these groups, detain persons and impose law. Although a peaceful hand-over of weapons had been agreed, the police came under heavy fire and those responsible were detained. Later that month, Muslim paramilitary units attacked Serbs and killed about 12 people, including women and children. Those responsible were detained. This is a short summary, and I don't have further questions at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hrsum, as you have noted while Mr. Karadzic read out the summary of your statement, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, and now you'll be further examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you remind me, please, of the exact date of the establishment of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: If you mean the SDS of Republika Srpska, I think it was in July in 1990, and the local municipal SDS organisation at Pale was established a little later, sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was the precise date in July of the SDS Republika Srpska party?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I think it was on the 12th, the 12th of July, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do -- can I assume correctly that the reason you are able to recall this date with such specificity is because you are a follower and/or member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the SDS at that time or later for that matter. In 1997, we members of the police had to have written certificates from the municipal parties saying that we were not members of any political party in order for us to do the job of policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since that time, Mr. Hrsum, have you become politically active in connection with or on behalf of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Now? I didn't understand your question. Throughout the time I was employed in the police, I was never politically active in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what translation you received. I said since that time. So after the period of time when you were -- when you had to provide a written certificate that you were not a member, after that time, did you become politically active in connection with or on behalf of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I did not become a member of the SDS. I did not become politically active, because in the course of 1998 and 1999, all the way until 2000, representatives of the international police certified members of the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, were you not on the list of SDS candidates for office in 2012 in your hometown or home municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I became politically active in the SDS two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hrsum, maybe in future questions you can try not to parse out my question with such -- with -- at that kind of level. I asked you at any time were you a member. That is the -- and you broke it down into the years in which you were not, ignoring this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me just call up 65 ter 24496 quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see there a list of candidates for the SDS party, and that is your name reflected at number 14; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6088, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hrsum, your statement indicates in various places and in various ways that the Muslims of Pale left the municipality voluntarily despite all efforts to make them stay and the efforts of the Pale police to protect them, and that's found, for example, in paragraph 22 where you talk about Muslims leaving voluntarily, or in paragraph 15 where you say the whole time Muslims in the Pale area were safe and went on with their regular activities. So is it your position, Mr. Hrsum, that there were no distinctions made, no discrimination against Muslims, no distinctions made between them and Serbs in Pale?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I assert that the Muslims at Pale were safe until they left voluntarily, until they changed their place of residence voluntarily. They were secure. Whether there were problems in certain enterprises or companies, discrimination against them, I can't say, but when it comes to the public security station and its employees, we were not aware of these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And further, according to you, the voluntary departure of Muslims from their homes or their places of business and so on began with or at least was reflected by the voluntary departure of the Muslim police from the Pale SJB; correct? That is, the departure of the Muslim police was also voluntary according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That's a compound question. I think it's better if he asks them one at a time as a yes answer would be ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Hrsum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand it well enough, because one part refers to the voluntary departure of Muslims from the Pale municipality, and the other refers to the termination of employment of Muslim policemen. These were two different events, and they were not mutually connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you could rephrase your question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you claim, as appears to be the case at paragraph 13 of your statement, Mr. Hrsum, that the Muslim police voluntarily stopped coming to work without explanation and then a meeting was organised and the Muslim police advised that they wanted to temporarily stop coming to work and handed in their weapons and official IDs on their own?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I have to give a rather lengthy reply to this question. Some of the Muslim policemen employed in the crime service where I worked, and there were two Muslims working there, left their jobs at the Pale police station in 1991, and the other one left sometime in early 1992. That's when they stopped coming to work at the Pale police station, which had procedures in force at the time relating to being moved from one organisational unit to another. That's as regards those two. Also, sometime in early 1992, in January, for inexplicable reasons the commander of the Pale police station, his name was Efendic, stopped coming to work. Efendic was his last name. I can't recall his first name at the moment. He did this for no reason. And some 10 days later, it was discovered that he had started work in the organisational unit of the MUP in Sarajevo. The -- another one who in early 1992 worked as a forensic technician was sent to the training centre for staff members in Vraca. That was a school where I had gone to which was later transformed into a training centre for staff members. So he was sent to a specialist course there and he never came back. Later on we learned that when he completed the course, he started work in the Stari Grad public security station. The procedure at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, that's more detail than necessary. Let me shortcut this by asking you whether the -- well, first of all let me say this: The time that you have given for the commander of the police station Efendic, stopping coming to work in January is contradicted by paragraph 13 of your statement where you place that event after such things as the referendum on independence and actually use a precise date of 17 March 1992. But to get to the heart of the matter, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think it's only fair to the witness that this be put to him for an answer, not to make it a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see your statement? Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger referred to paragraph 13 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me -- in fairness to the witness, Mr. President, the date of March 17th refers to the Muslim police in the Pale area and the reference to Efendic is more amorphous, indicating simply that they were preceded in that by Efendic. I'm going to withdraw that comparison and simply ask, if I may, and simply ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, is it your position then, without regard to the specifics of how you claim some Muslims left, that the Pale police, the Serbian members of the Pale police, did not disarm the non-Serb police employees and remove them from service? Do you deny that that happened?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No. No. That did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention then to a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First I'd like to turn to 65 ter 01495. The second page of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is a report of the 24th of March, 1992, from the joint MUP Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, referring to the removal of policemen of Muslim nationality from the Pale and Sokolac Public Security Stations on 23 March. It indicates the number of policemen, talks about events at Pale involving the chief of the SUP, Mr. Koroman, and six active-duty policemen with rifles, and Mr. Koroman's claim that the removal of these Muslim policemen was a counter-measure against a move made by the Stari Grad Public Security Station in Sarajevo. And then the report goes on to note that a mixed commission was formed in the joint MUP to examine those claims. Mr. Hrsum, this document is a reflection, is it not, of events in March when in fact policemen of Muslim nationality were removed from service by Mr. Koroman and the Serbian members of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Well, what you say does not correspond to the facts. Employees of Muslim nationality asked for a meeting, six or seven of them who had remained, because, as I have already explained, the others had left individually, one by one. They asked for a meeting with the management. It was requested by Abdulah Kadrovic [phoen] who was in the Pale local commune. After this meeting, they expressed a wish to not have to come to work temporarily, and they explained this by the problems that had arisen in the city of Sarajevo and some other municipalities where there had been some forcible disarming of members of the Serb police, and they insisted on this. They were very persistent. This Abdulah Kadrovic, who was a very good policeman and very influential in the Pale police station, on behalf of all these other policemen kept explaining that they would have to stop coming to work on a temporary basis, and they asked the chief and commander of the police station to approve this. And it was approved, but they had -- because, of course, when a policeman is temporarily not doing their job, he has to give back his badge and his personal official weapons. As for their private weapons, if they had hunting weapons or something like that, they did not have to give that back nor was it taken from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, you say "what you say," meaning me, "does not correspond to the facts," but of course I was showing you a contemporaneous document produced at the time, immediately after those events. But let me not show you only a document of the joint MUP, but let's see what the Pale SJB of Republika Srpska had to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I do that, Mr. President, I would tender the last document, 65 ter 01495.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6089, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the document you're about to see, Mr. Hrsum, is dated the 8th of February, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, did I not -- I apologise for that. 65 ter 24483.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could you zoom in a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see from the header, Mr. Hrsum, this is a document of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior Public Security Station Pale, dated 8 February 1993, and it's a record in connection with the hand-over from the former chief to the new SJB chief. And it states: "According to its records, in the course of 1992, the police station did the following: "Due to the security reasons in mid-March, the police station disarmed the non-Serb police employees and removed them from service." So, Mr. Hrsum, this in fact is the -- or the subsequent account by the Pale police station itself about the removal of those policemen, and this is in fact the accurate account of what happened to these police officers, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No. That's not how it happened. As I understand it, this is a report of the police station commander compiled because of the hand-over to another chief of the police station where he mentioned the events that had taken place, but why he described them in this way, I don't know. These things didn't all happen all in March. Members of the Muslim ethnicity, it was only on the 22nd of May, 1992, that their weapons began to be taken away, first of all in the Renovica municipality and then in other places. So this really does not correspond to the real truth. And those six or seven policemen employed at the Pale Public Security Station did not represent any kind of security threat, so I don't know why this was formulated in the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you've alluded to, Mr. Hrsum, the document also notes that weapons owned by non-Serb citizens were seized and that was irrespective of whether the owners had permits for them or not, that is, whether the weapons were legally possessed or not. That's another difference between what you said and what this document, official document by the Pale SJB, provides.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I can only repeat that those policemen who were of Muslim ethnicity who voluntarily handed over their weapons, I think this was in the second half of March or the beginning of the second half of March, they did not have their personal or hunting weapons taken away if they had proper licenses for those weapons. As for the citizens of non-Serb ethnicity, it was only on the 22nd of May that their weapons began to be confiscated. It says here that this was done in -- around the middle of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at some other contemporaneously produced documents, Mr. Hrsum, and contrast that -- those documents to what you have asserted in your statement, again now focusing on your claim that the Muslims of Pale left their homes, their livelihoods, and made themselves refugees voluntarily. This Court, Mr. Hrsum, has already received evidence that at the time that these events were taking place in 1992, the president of the Crisis Staff of Pale advised a member of the collective Presidency of Republika Srpska and one of the war commissioners that Muslims were being forcibly moved out, including through a large number of illegal and criminal actions. Now, I'll -- you're welcome to see that document if you want. The Court just -- and the parties just saw that recently, but let me ask you if you are aware of the fact that the president of the Crisis Staff, who was also the president of the Executive Committee, was saying that at the time such events were taking place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I am personally not aware of this, and I think it was not known in the public security station either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm referring to P6034, Mr. President, and I believe it's a document of July 7th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd also like to look at what the contemporaneous documentation revealed about the role of the police in moving Muslims out. And in that connection, Mr. Hrsum, although you asserted just now that you were not aware -- aware of it and think it was not known in the public security station either, this Court has also recently received evidence - that's D00031 - that in a meeting of the Municipal Assembly on 18 June 1992, the president of the Assembly and the chairman of the Executive Committee, who was also the president of the Crisis Staff, objected to the activities of the public security station in this respect, that is, during the course of discussion about Muslims moving out, because it had participated in the attempt to organise the Muslims and move them out. Mr. Hrsum, according to the president of the Assembly of the municipality, according to the president of the Executive Committee, who was also president of the Crisis Staff, the Pale police were involved in efforts to organise the Muslims and move them out. That was actually the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: There was an Assembly meeting in the second half of the month of June, when conditions were in place for the meeting to take place, and after that the Crisis Staff was disbanded. After the marathon session of the Assembly, a decision was made that those Muslims who wanted to change their place of residence should be allowed to do so. That decision was made, and the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly sent a written note to the public security station. They asked us to put in place conditions and undertake measures for the secure departure of all those who wanted to leave, and we were supposed to make sure that they crossed the separation line safely. The public security station never participated in any discussions as to whether the Muslims should leave Pale or not. The only involvement was for us to provide security for all the Muslims in Pale, bearing in mind the circumstances and the times as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also take some pains in your statement to credit the police with conscientiously and scrupulously protecting non-Serbs, including following through on investigations of crimes against non-Serbs. And I think we can find that in paragraph 23, referring -- that begins with alleged incidents committed by Muslims against Serbs which were reported to the investigating judge in Sokolac, but which then goes on to cite several incidents in which Muslims were victims and assert that criminal investigations were duly conducted. And in particular, you cite the case of the murder of Muharem Hasna and Ramiz Kujovic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I heard you say, "Da," but perhaps you can confirm that to the interpreter. She didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: It is correct that those individuals were killed in Pale, and those killings --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, sorry, I appreciated the fact that you responded by acknowledging that you had said that in your statement, because I want to get on to another aspect. I didn't want you to explain that in detail just yet because I do want to look at what actually happened with that investigation. And the reason I want to look at that is because, contrary to the suggestion in paragraph 3 about the scrupulous performance of duty by the Pale police in connection with this incident, there was severe criticism by the chief of the criminal investigation service for not -- for the not proper investigation and fulfilment of their completion of the investigation in connection with that event, and in particular, you were criticised for that, Mr. Hrsum. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I don't remember that I was criticised, but I remember the incident. Those people of Muslim ethnicity were killed, and the investigation was carried out by the investigating judge from Sokolac. The records of the investigation and further instructions were in the hands of the investigating judge. At that time, pursuant to the regulations that were in effect in our area, it was an investigating judge who carried out an on-site inspection, compiled the records of that, and based on all those documents, photographic evidence and everything else that could possibly be collected on the spot in view of the technical shortcomings were then forwarded to the investigating judge and then the investigating judge would then forward the material to the prosecutor who then decided whether any other measures should be undertaken or, alternatively, there was enough to issue an indictment and continue with the procedure. That was the procedure that was in place. Such on-site inspections were carried out by an investigating judge accompanied by police members, and all that was done at our request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hrsum, I think the answer to the question I had asked was no, you don't remember that you were criticised. For future questions, I would appreciate it if we could follow a question-and-answer format.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me, then, turn to 65 ter 24148 which is a report on activities of the criminal investigation service in the period between 1 April and 31 December 1992. If we could turn, please, to page 4 of the English and also 4 of the B/C/S. Scroll down toward the bottom. That report states, and I'll just read two pertinent sections at the -- toward the bottom of the first full paragraph on page 4 of the English and toward the -- in the second-to-last paragraph on -- in the B/C/S. It states -- here it says: "Toco Hrsun," but if you look at the B/C/S, you can clearly see it's "Tomo Hrsum," as we can see from later entries, "did not write the official report in connection with the murder of Hasna Kujovic, the report in connection with the damage caused by a hand-grenade thrown into the Sandro [phoen] bar, and neither did he take the written statement from Predrag Vojnovic about the circumstances of the traffic accident he had caused or the statement of the injured party." And it continues with similar criticisms on the next page, in the middle of page 5 of the English and toward the bottom of the next page in B/C/S. "In the same vein, Tomo Hrsum interrogated several persons who participated in the crime of forcible entry and theft into a shop in Praca, but he never finished the case so that a criminal report was never submitted or registered in spite of the significant material damage."
