And it goes on to note you are "carrying out certain tasks that were never reported to anyone without having done anything concrete, no effect."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, focusing specifically on the murder of Hasna Kujovic, which you cite in your statement, this official report on the activities of the criminal investigation service, Mr. Hrsum, states that, in fact, you didn't write the official report in connection with that murder and criticises that failure as a problem of the service; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: That report was written, and it was sent to the investigating judge, without that report -- without all the necessary documentation that should have been obtained from the doctor who inspected the body, because that was all that we could do. We did not have an expert that could have carried a post-mortem. So all that was forwarded. It was all registered, and that report is in the files of the prosecutor, and I suppose that the prosecutor forwarded all that to the investigating judge who then ordered certain other measures that needed to be carried out. I believe that exists in the archives of the prosecutor's office. It may have happened that the report was not immediately compiled because there was a medical report pending, photo documentation had to be prepared. At that time we did not have a forensic technician who could do that. Before the war we had a forensic technician. He was a Muslim, but he left the public security station in January. Everything, however, was done and sent to the prosecutor's office in the form of a report, and that was all registered in the log-book that was kept at the public security station. I believe that that log-book still exists and that all that can be verified even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it -- it hadn't -- it certainly hadn't been completed by this date. It hadn't been completed by December 5th when -- and the problem with not completing it, the problem with the fact that you didn't write that official report means that the report doesn't get submitted to the public prosecutor; right? A?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, I'd like to look at 65 ter 18828.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the witness can be given a chance to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to direct his attention to something very indirectly and then give him a chance to answer the question. I think that's the more efficient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, would you like to comment on Mr. Tieger's statement just now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say. I've already told you that we had to wait for an order from the judge as to whether to do something else. We had to wait for the doctor's report on visual inspection, and based on that, we compiled our report and sent it to the prosecutor's office. There were crimes that could not be registered immediately in the log-book, because some facts had to be collected to point to a reasonable doubt that existed. When reasonable suspicion was established, then we forwarded information to the prosecutor's office in the form of a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the reality is, Mr. Hrsum, that the head of the criminal investigation service, the head of criminal investigations, criticised the failure to write the official report, not only the document we've just seen but in the document I was just about to show you, 65 ter 18828. Okay. And if we look at the bottom of the page, we can see the following: [As read] "Tomo Hrsum, an inspector in the criminal service did not complete a large number of cases. He did not write an official report on the investigation of murder of Hasna Kujovic and the investigation on site was completed in 1992 by the investigating judge and employees of this SJB, which means that the report has never been submitted to the Sokolac municipal public prosecutor." And the date of this document is December 5th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: This does not tally with any of the facts. There is a report with all the necessary documents. The SJB Pale sent all that to the prosecutor's office. The investigating judge also attached his report. All that was recorded in the log-book, and a copy of that exists at the Pale SJB. This does not correspond with the truth. I really don't know what kind of report is this. I don't know who drafted this, who -- who it was sent to, who verified this. What is this report about? I would like somebody to explain to me. Since I was the chief of the crime prevention services and if a report was written about the work of that service, it had to be sent to the chief and to the superior of the organ because that report would have been written by the SJB and the administration for administrative affairs and then it was sent to the officer in charge. And based on that, an annual report would be drafted. I don't know what is -- what this is. If this is an annual report that had to be sent to the higher instances within the MUP. I really don't know what this is. What kind of report is this? I don't know who it was sent to. Every report had to be stamped. It had to be signed. Is this stamped? Is this signed? Is this a statement? What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we turn to the last page, we can see that it's dated the 5th of December, 1993. It says: "Report written by Stjepan Micic." At the stop of the page -- well, let's see very quickly. At the top of the page, the first page, it indicates: "Composed by the head of the service, Mr. Micic," and then it was followed by the report on the 31st of December that we previously saw. And in that connection, let me just turn quickly to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What's the date of this document, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can find it on the last page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And which is? Is it not May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That would be correct. My apologies for that misreading of the date, or misstatement of the date. 1993 is what I meant to say instead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know Stjepan Micic, Mr. Hrsum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to interrupt the Court's questions, but I was -- in that regard I was going to turn to 65 ter 24485, which is a list of Pale police station members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let's hear from the witness about this document. Now you see that there is signature of Micic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Micic's signature here and I can see that that report was written on the 12th of May, 1993. A report on the work of the crime prevention services and the report on the police organs and departments within the SJB were issued on a monthly, three monthly, and biannual basis. They would be drafted on the 1st of January, the 1st of April, and then there would be the biannual report which was written on the 1st of July. All those reports had to have a heading, the addressee. If that was a proper report. If it was just something that an individual did for his own pleasure, it didn't have to. Every such report had to be stamped and signed by the person who drafted it, but with the Court's leave, I would like to provide another comment if I may. Perhaps some things about Mr. Micic. On the eve of the war he arrived at the SJB. He -- some five or ten days before the war broke out, he was appointed by the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's where he worked. All that time that he was at the SJB, he always had problems. He was a man who had graduated from the school of political sciences. He was a journalist and he didn't know much about the policing and the police work. He didn't know what was necessary, what facts were necessary to collect in order to establish that there was reasonable suspicion that a crime was committed. I can see an example here. My conversation or -- with several individuals in Praca. It is true at that we brought those individuals in, that we took their written statements and we interviewed them, but there was not an aggrieved party. There were no damages. We could not interview all the persons at the same time over a short period of time. We could not bring them in in such a short period of time because there were a lot of people who had stolen goods from a shop, and that shop was socially owned, and those goods were taken away. And based on the statements that we collected and that were for the large part denied by the individuals who were suspected as the perpetrators of the crimes, we did not have any grounds to send all that to the prosecutor in the form of a crime report because all that would have been returned to us by the prosecutor's office or rejected by him. It was not common practice to do that. Conditions had to be put in place for the proper facts to be collected in order to point out that a crime was indeed perpetrated by certain individuals. Based on the indicia that we had at that time, we could not draft a criminal report. That's why I don't understand who did this and who that person sent it to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, could you speak a bit -- a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you don't have to be nervous and just concentrate on the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd tender those last two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to be clear, I think we haven't had any -- tender -- this is three documents. I'm not sure if we're -- 24481, 18828, and I'm not sure if he's offering 24485. In any event, we no objection to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having noted down two documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, since -- I was going to pass on that. We can call up 24485 very quickly. It's a list that wasn't shown to the witness yet and just he can confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First document, could you give the number again, RS MUP report, end-of-year report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 24481, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P6091 and P6092 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could quickly call 24485.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, if you could just confirm that that is your name that appears there as well as Mr. Micic and other members of the Pale SJB, including the chief, Malko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P6093. Almost done, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I noticed that, Mr. President. I have three discrete areas -- well, actually more like two areas. One of which is -- is quite brief and specific and I'll try to move through those as quickly as possible, if I may. I think they're areas the Court would want to hear about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Reid had provided me with a note indicating when the allotted time had been up, but we were in the middle of a discussion and I -- although I asked him to do so so I could note it specifically for the Court, I failed to do so. So thank you for bringing that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, I want to look at one other aspect of the Pale police's monitoring of and responding to any crimes against Muslims. And in that connection, I'd like to turn to paragraph 17 of your statement where you refer to the Muslims, the hundreds of Muslims, who arrived from Bratunac, and as Mr. Karadzic says in his summary, were hosted by the -- by Pale authorities in Pale. In paragraph 17, Mr. Micic -- Mr. Hrsum, you state: "There is no record or information that these citizens had been abused during their stay in Pale." Do you know, Mr. Hrsum, whether or not these -- or first of all, do you claim that these 400 people, that none of these 400 people had been abused at any time prior to their arrival in Pale, or during their stay in Pale, or as they were being escorted to their ultimate destination from Pale?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Before they arrived at Pale, I can't say whether they were ill-treated, whether they were subjected to some illegal measures. I can claim that during their stay at Pale, which was for about 48 hours, no repressive measures were applied against any individual by the police. Until the moment they were provided security for the convoy, those people did not suffer any abuse. There were about 400 of them. I don't know the exact number, but I believe that there were about 400 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you say there was no record or information, but this Trial Chamber has repeatedly seen the video evidence of what these people looked like upon their arrival in Visoko. And I understand that our video capabilities are limited today, but I don't think there'll be any dispute among the parties if I say that those people were visibly beaten and bruised and gashed and limping and some -- one unable to hold down any water, and in short, they were manifestly abused. Now, Mr. Hrsum, that took place either before they arrived at Pale, while they were in Pale, or after they left Pale under escort. Are you saying the Pale police never became aware of the beatings and abuse that these people suffered?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The Pale police did not investigate whether those people had been mistreated earlier on and whether they had went through any unpleasant situations prior to their arrival at Pale. As of the moment when they arrived there and as of the moment when the president of the municipality spoke to those who escorted them from Bratunac, I can claim with certainty that no one at Pale undertook any repressive or provocative measures against those people. They were accommodated in Pale, and they were placed in the sports hall of the Romanija club. And since the premises were not too large, some of them even slept on the buses. The buses were secured because they were in the vicinity of the police station. We even organised that food be brought from the barracks at Pale. The same kind of food was being delivered to the policemen on duty in the station, meaning they enjoyed the same kind of food, and I claim that with certainty. Our police did not take part in escorting them to their final destination. The public security station personnel verified what route was to be taken. All routes were cut off. They found a safe route through the forest in order to bring them from Pale down to Ilijas. That was the task that the police station took -- undertook upon itself. The next day the route was checked in order to verify whether it was safe and whether the buses can pass through. These were very narrow forest and village roads. That was the task of the Pale Public Security Station. The following day the people were transported. Now, whether they had been mistreated before that or not, all I can say is that they were dressed partly in civilian clothes and partly in military close. Some of them had military jackets or military pants, whereas the rest of their clothes would be civilian. Now, whether they had been mistreated or not, that's something I can't say, and the public security station at Pale did not attempt to obtain information of any potential mistreatment earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it that as far as you know, no one was ever punished for what happened to these people.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I don't know whether someone was punished in Bratunac and whether such people may have been from the military or civilian authorities. All I know is that there were no problems at Pale. If I may, it was explained to the authorities in Pale and to the police that those Muslims wanted to go to Central Bosnia. Whether that was true or not, I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We just talked about what happened at the time of the arrival of the Bratunac -- the hundreds of people from Bratunac. Do you claim that the members of the Pale police never beat people in custody at any time during 1992? And in particular, I'm referring to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you mean the citizens from Bratunac or some other Muslims who were temporarily in the Romanija sports hall?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I was explicitly trying to move away from the event involving the hundreds of people from Bratunac since you express some views on that, but I was asking you if you claim that Muslims were never beaten at any other time in 1992 while in the custody of the police.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that perhaps there were no abuses by those who secured the premises or that maybe they allowed entry to certain individuals. As for the leadership of the Pale police station, it was never made aware of it. They were never notified by either those who guarded any people or the people who were there, who were occasionally visited by the chief of police. There were strict orders that no person can enter the premises unless approved by the chief of the police station. Whether there were any abuses is something I can't say, but I can say something else: If that had been known, if that had been established, measures would have been taken definitely against the employees who secured the sports hall and against those who attempted to enter the premises. That's what I can say with certainty. As for anything else, I cannot be certain. In any case, the authorities tried to prevent unauthorised entry by all means. As for the policemen of the public security station at Pale, I dare claim that they did not undertake any repressive measures against the people detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Please try to heed the Court's suggestion about the length of the answers, sir. What about you, Mr. Hrsum? This Trial Chamber has received evidence, in fact - that's in P00733 - that you were personally involved in beating Muslim detainees.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you think of any reason why anybody would single you out from other policemen as being a person involved in beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask Mr. Tieger to show the document to the witness and mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course he will come to that, but I would like you not to interfere with the lines of questions from the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you recall the last question I asked, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I do recall your last question. I don't know who that could have been or why they would say that. I claim that I have never taken part in such activities, and I never entered the room where those people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at P730 -- 00733, paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's fair to put it to the witness. Was it admitted under seal or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I was actually calling it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was Mr. Crncalo's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sulejman Crncalo. Okay. It gives the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to give him -- show the next page for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you've read that portion, sir, we're moving on to the next page which contains the bulk of that paragraph. And then just to continue, in paragraph 24 it notes that Mr. Koroman arrived and recognised Mr. Crncalo and ordered Mr. Hrsum from the room. That's what's alleged, sir. Do you claim that wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: It is me, but this is not true, and the sequence of events is not described as it should be. I recall having seen this statement. It's even on the internet. This statement is inaccurate in describing how it developed and why. I don't know if you want me to expand. I simply wanted to say that the employees of the crime service in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time never wore uniforms and did not have batons that he mentions here. All of the equipment crime officers had was the official ID, the official sidearm, and handcuffs. There were no batons ever issued to the employees of the crime service or any uniforms until the war began when we were issued with standard issue military uniforms that we also wore at the front lines. Mr. Crncalo was brought by Mr. Koroman, the chief of station, into my office. He was taken in by some policemen, and he wanted to speak to Mr. Koroman first. He brought him in to the office and said that a statement should be taken since he was found with a weapon, a hunting rifle. It seemed that his possession of that weapon was against the law. It was a type of misdemeanour, as a matter of fact. It did not qualify as a crime. That is why he was released. As for the other person, he did not have a weapon on him at the moment of being brought in to the police station. Once the interview in the police station was over, the same Mr. Koroman, because they frequently talked to him and he represented himself as a Muslim representative, trying to give an impression that he could speak for the Muslim side, and they frequently met in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention for the transcript. We don't have the end of the sentence. The witness said that Malko Koroman put them in his own vehicle and took them home to their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have one more very discrete area, and that arises from paragraph 15 of your statement, sir, in which you say: "In mid-April, the RS Presidency established the Territorial Defence as the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of BH which was not mobilised since these forces were mobilised at a later date." The fact is, sir, and -- that an imminent threat of war and a general public mobilisation was ordered on the entire territory of the RS by the republic officials, and in that case by Mr. Subotic, on the 16th of April, 1992, right in mid-April, the time you say it was first formed and not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's P02412. If we could turn to that quickly. As we see at the bottom, the decision, a general public mobilisation has been ordered on the entire territory of Serbian BH, and that document is dated the 16th of April, 1992. Further, if we turn to the next page in English, and the next page in B/C/S as well, it provides a statement of reasons. It further provides that the municipal Territorial Defence Staffs that have operated regularly so far shall remain in the same formation and establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Hrsum, contrary to the suggestion in your statement, Pale was one of those municipalities where the municipal TO staff was already operating regularly; correct? By that date.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Relatively speaking. There were Muslim employees in those staffs as well who sometimes were there and sometimes were not. At some point there was even some talk of missing documents. I can't confirm that. It was just a rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, in early April, the Pale municipality staff was not only functioning, but it was operating in such a manner as to be engaged in military activity against the old part of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No. The TO staff did not take part in the operation aimed at Sarajevo. When the first clashes erupted on the 6th -- well, the territory of Stari Grad municipality and the border with the municipality of Srpski, Serbian Stari Grad, those two settlements have a clear division between them, between the Serbian and Muslim settlement. The moment there were problems, the Serbian citizens who live in the direction of the Srpski Stari Grad municipality, they set up positions and asked for help and asked that members of TO units joined them. However, at the time, the TO did not have any units. There was a barracks in Pale where Serb citizens reported to mobilisation which was issued by the JNA. They were trying to man their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, that was long answer. I trust you've -- I haven't asked you about everything the TO was doing. I asked you about whether or not they engaged in military activity against the old part of Sarajevo. I think you've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, I'd like to turn to 65 ter 15577. This is a document of the command of the 2nd Military District dated the 8th of April, 1992. And if we turn to page 2 of the English and we see item under 4th Corps. It's on page 1 of the B/C/S. It provides or it -- it states that: "During the afternoon, the members of the Territorial Defence from Pale municipality opened ... fire on the sector of Vratnik and on the old part of the city of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a contemporaneous reflection of the reality of what was happening with respect to the Pale TO, Mr. Hrsum, that is in contravention of what you've just told us; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Looking at the report, one would say so. Fire was opened. There was sporadic shooting. At the time, the Pale police station also sent in a reinforced patrol to a check-point. The check-point was at the location where a check-point had been agreed upon between the public security station chief at Pale and the public security station chief at Stari Grad. The people who self-organised and who set up guards exchanged fire. There was even mortar fire as far as I know and according to what those policemen who were there at the check-point told us. Well, that was simply not in their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President, except to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have about seven minutes before the break, Mr. Karadzic. Would you like to start your re-examination, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, Your Excellency, but I'll need more than seven minutes. Perhaps it is a good time for a break. The last break was also a little bit early. Perhaps this one could be too. I'll be able to conclude my cross-examination after the break -- my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 10 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a brief question for you, Mr. Robinson, in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bring in the next witness. While we're doing that, Mr. Robinson, having heard the overall estimated length of the cross-examination for General Milosevic, I wonder whether you are now in the position to tell us when we'll hear the evidence of Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We actually made a filing just a few minutes ago of our weekly witness list for next week but we're proposing that General Krstic be heard on either Wednesday afternoon or Thursday after the testimony of Mr. Trifkovic and Garaplija. So we are estimating that on Tuesday the cross-examination, and hopefully the redirect, could be completed for General Milosevic. And then on Wednesday we would have Mr. Trifkovic, Mr. Garaplija, and if there is any time left over that day, General Krstic, and if not, we would have General Krstic the next day. And I've also notified his lawyer of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And from next week we are supposed to move to Courtroom III, but while we are hearing evidence of Mr. Milosevic, we will remain in Courtroom I. And I appreciate the assistance, co-operation of the Chamber that hears the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hrsum, you were shown document P6 in relation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6090. Now it's all right in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 40 of today's transcript, lines 1 to 6, you mentioned the events in the public security station of Stari Grad which influenced the events at Pale. In your statement, in paragraph 7 you say that the SDS won a landslide victory at Pale. Did the SDS share power with the SDA party at Pale?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes. It shared power with the SDA at Pale so that the deputy of the president of the municipality was a Muslim. That was how they agreed to share power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these inter-party agreements concern other government bodies and services such as the police, for example?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes, but it was only afterwards, only later that these agreements had to do with the MUP of Republika Srpska. However, in the public security station of Pale, there was never a division of the police station between the Muslim part and the Serb part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hrsum, I'm interested in the pre-war period now. Why was Stari Grad mentioned? Was there an agreement in Stari Grad for there to be a similar division of posts as in the police as at Pale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's -- excuse me. Maybe it's relatively harmless in context, but it should be -- it's rather inappropriate to ask the question and then answer it in the -- immediately afterwards in the submission to the witness. So I'd discourage that form of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, can you then tell me why on page 40, during today's cross-examination, you mentioned the Stari Grad Public Security Station in connection with events at the Pale Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: In all the stations and before these agreements were made the ethnic composition of the policemen reflected the ethnic composition of the local population. In Sarajevo, there was a certain number of policemen doing their jobs, but in mid-February they were simply disarmed and chased out of the Stari Grad police station, and they arrived at the Pale police station. However, they did not carry on their work on the territory of the Pale Public Security Station but were instead sent to do that work in the part of the Stari Grad municipality in Sarajevo which was mostly Serb as regards population, and that was Vucija Luka and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly look at D386 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document and tell us who issued it and what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: This document was issued by the Stari Grad Public Security Station in Sarajevo, and it refers to the situation and the impossibility to work of members of the Serb ethnicity in that police station, and it talks about how they're at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ismet Dahic is mentioned and the Green Berets in point 2. Can you tell us what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Well, when the reserve police force was mobilised following orders from the minister of the interior, in the Stari Grad police station parts of members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets were mobilised, and the chief of the station and the commander of the station co-operated with the command of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, and they were even together with active-duty policemen at the check-points. I'm referring to policemen from Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the last page to see how many Serb policemen signed this.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I can't see the number very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: About 20?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Some 20 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, was it the custom when someone was received into the reserve police force or the regular police force to check up on these people, and were these members of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League scrutinised in this sense?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Before the war, for someone to be part of the reserve police force they had to be subjected to a check. It couldn't be someone who had been convicted of a crime or who was being tried for a crime or even for a misdemeanour with the exception of some traffic violations and so on. There were teachers and doctors who were in the reserve police force and eminent people. However, the persons who were in the Green Berets and the Patriotic League who entered the reserve police force in Stari Grad municipality were not subjected to such checks. I had been employed in the crime prevention service for a long time, and I knew that -- among them were even persons who were known to the police and who were prone to committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hrsum. After the war you worked until 2001, as it says in paragraph 1 of your statement. Did you have to go through a security check? Did you have to be certified? You just mentioned that the ITPF certifies policemen.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Well, ITPF certified the police in Republika Srpska on two occasions. The first time was in late 1997 and early 1998, and there was a rigorous certification of the police of Republika Srpska by the IE [as interpretation] Federation sometime in 2000. I personally went through this certification process, and I have the certificate at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These events in Stari Grad municipality, which is neighbouring to Pale, how did it -- how was it reflected in the police station at Pale? You spoke about this on page 40 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The events in the Stari Grad Public Security Station had repercussions in the security station in Pale. There were comments, unlawful acts. However, nothing changed in the work of the Pale Public Security Station. It continued to function in the same way as before, and all communications went through the city SUP and the security centre, and those persons who had arrived were sent to the area of these neighbourhoods which were inhabited by Serbs where a municipality was established later on, and there was a single station, department there, set up there, which was -- actually came under the command of the Pale Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on pages 41 and 42, you said that document 56090 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: P6090, sorry, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- you said that what was stated was not correct because the chronological sequence of events was incorrectly described and that the Muslims were not disarmed in March but in May 1992. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let's have a look at D16. D16, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date here and what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: This refers to the speech made by Malko Koroman in the public media, that is, in a TV broadcast, because in the community centre at Pale police -- a television station was started, and the Muslims were to hand over their weapons. There was a consequence of the situation in the Renovica local commune when a police tactical action was carried out to disarm Muslims when two police officers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document, P6090, does it say that citizens of Muslim ethnicities were disarmed in March, and before this, was there any disarming of Muslims before the 22nd of May, and why was this order issued -- or, rather, what was the occasion for what happened on the 22nd of May, when those people from Renovica had to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Well, there were several things that influenced the planning and implementation of the tactical police action. One of these was that in the Renovica area, there were armed persons in uniform moving about, and up to that point such uniforms had not been seen in the former Yugoslavia. The second reason for this action was that there were frequent reports by the military security organs to the effect that there were incursions and constant attacks and incursions in the Renovica barracks, which was in the centre of Renovica, and at the perimeter of this area there were three or four villages from which equipment and materiel were removed. This includes weapons, ammunition, explosive devices, and so on. The third reason was that in the Renovica area, there were two persons who could be linked to a murder which had taken place before the war broke out, and the corpse was found in the Pale area, but the place where the crime was perpetrated and the perpetrator could not be found. However, based on a report from the security centre in Sarajevo, we knew that these two people were the last to be seen with the victim while he was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a member of the police, were you informed about the arming, the new arming that was taking place on the territory of your municipality, and did the police demand that these weapons be handed over?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, the police had information about the distribution of weapons to Muslims. And on three occasions, the police took action with representatives of the security services who were in charge of these actions, because they joined in these actions to detect criminal offences and submit criminal reports. There was other information about this, but it was just indicia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript it's been transcribed differently. Was that the CSB, and what CSB was -- had jurisdiction over Pale, and was it involved in detecting illegal arming?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The CSB of Sarajevo with its headquarters in Sarajevo was responsible for several municipalities in the Sarajevo area. Its operative purview was broader in territorial terms than just the SUP of Sarajevo, and their employees were always involved in investigating serious crimes, or if a public security station needed assistance and asked for assistance from employees of the CSB. In Pale we regularly informed the CSB and asked for their assistance. Until -- this was all until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall a name of a person who participated in the dissemination and concealment of weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: In one case it was Dulovic, a soldier who was at the barracks in Renovica. That barracks was actually a depot of equipment and materiel more than barracks for a combat unit or troops. This Renovic [as interpreted], together with some other persons from the Podgrab, Praca and Renovica municipalities, was detained, and this was something that the military security organs in the Victor Bubanj barracks were in charge of. After this, there was a protest by members of the Muslim ethnic group both in Pale and Sarajevo. The second instance was when a hodza - that is a representative of the religious community - who was carrying out his religious duty in the Praca area, and he had a TAM vehicle, and in his vehicle, based on a report, weapons were found. A third instance was very telling. It was a shop selling sports equipment in the Pale area, and this happened in early 1991. The person who was running that shop was selling weapons and also giving away weapons and without the buyers of the weapons obtaining licenses beforehand. And he did not make lists of these people, nor did he inform the police station of these sales, and he had to do that in order for those persons to get licenses to carry weapons. And employees of the CSB participated in this, and those persons, in order to say that there is -- to reduce their responsibility said that they had been doing this with the approval of people from the MUP, and they mentioned certain names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He mentioned Avdo Hebib. It seems the name did not make it into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at D14. D14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An imam is referred to, a Muslim priest. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 28th of April. Mr. Hrsum, is the name of Senaid Memic mentioned, from Hrasnica, who distributed the weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes, he is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today my learned friend Mr. Tieger suggested to you that based on the unsigned document which was not issued as part of the standard protocol, the disarming took place in March. Before these weapons were discovered on the 28th of April and after the 22nd of May, were Muslims disarmed? Were they disarmed before this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The Muslim population was not being disarmed before this date. They were not disarmed on this occasion either, at least not all of them. Before the war Fazlo Gljiva took part in distributing and forwarding weapons. Allegedly, he submitted an anonymous report actually reporting himself. He stated the weapons were on his vehicle as he sold some and gave away some. There was all -- basically a clash among the members of the Muslim community because some received weapons for free from him, whereas others paid a lot, and they were dissatisfied with Gljiva's behaviour. In order to protect himself and as we were told by the CSB, he reported that the weapons were in his vehicle. This was only later when Fazlo, aka Gljiva, returned. For a while he was absent. Once he returned, he wanted to settle accounts with those who caused trouble for him later on. So he informed certain people at the public security station to go and collect such weapons. This was not the process of disarmament of the Muslim population en masse such as the one which followed the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today at pages 43 and 44 of the transcript, my learned friend Mr. Tieger suggested to you -- or actually, you answered that departure was made possible only to -- for those Muslims who wanted it; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D31, please, Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the document? Is the date the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Pardon me. Could we please zoom in? The document is the minutes of a session of the Pale Municipal Assembly. This one was held on the 18th of June, 1992. Actually, the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that is actually two and a half months after the outbreak of war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes, exactly two and a half months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 4, item 2. We'll see whether the same goes for the English version. Item 2. Can we please locate it in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what was decided here. The decision-making process is described, as well as the discussion which preceded it.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it was decided to approve the requests of Muslims who wanted to change their places of residence on a temporary basis. It pertained to all those who wanted to move, and it was decided only after a marathon session. I think this particular session lasted for 15 or 16 hours. It was based on their request and based on the lists which they brought in themselves on two or three occasions that they were allowed to leave. They asked the Municipal Assembly at Pale to approve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You pointed out that it was a temporary change of residence. As regards our law, is there a difference between a permanent and temporary place of residence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: These were two different terms when describing a citizen's status. A permanent place of residence entailed being registered with the competent police station where he or she would be issued with an ID, passport, or any other document they may have required in order to exercise their rights that they could enjoy in the given place of residence. The temporary place of residence is temporary. It happened once people moved from their permanent place of residence to another location where they stayed temporarily, either for education, work, or other personal needs. They were duty-bound to report their new place of residence within 15 days to the competent police station. They did not have to deregister from their original municipality. It sufficed that one brought in his or her ID and explained why they wanted to stay in the area. They would be issued a certificate stating that the person in question was to reside in the area for a specified period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it actually mean that it meant moving permanently?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today in document P6091, you could see that -- actually, it was suggested to you on the basis of that document that you did not undertake any investigations and did not submit any criminal reports for the murder of Vujovic and that you did not submit a report. You said that it was incorrect; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You explained at some length the sequence of activities. Perhaps you can tell me this: When does an investigating judge appear? Once he is included in the process, what is the police role as of that moment on?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The role of the police is to collect operational information in order to detect the perpetrator and to follow the investigating judge's orders in view of certain measures that he deemed necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at D2851 in e-court. It is a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, what is being forwarded?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Copies of the crime register documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 7 in the Serbian and 45 in the English. Zoom in, please. Could the other participants be left with the English version, whereas I'd like myself and the witness to be able to see the Serbian only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is in the first column, report, the second, reported, and then we have the dates; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is in entry 22?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: It is a case file forwarded to the municipal public prosecutor's office for the murder of Muharem Kujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who reported it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By having done that, was the case file effectively handed over to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes, formally and legally speaking. However, it was up to the public security station to undertake all measures within its competence in order to discover the perpetrator. This case file was not closed by virtue of having sent it to -- the entire case file, that is, that was necessary to be forwarded to the judiciary, but it was still upon the SJB to undertake its measures in order to discover the perpetrator or some other facts pertaining to the crime in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does this tally with the position expressed in document P69 -- 6091, where it is stated that you did not do what you were supposed to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: What do I know? It's probably not true what's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is stated there that you didn't submit a report concerning Haso.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: We submitted a report in the case of Haso as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 8 in the Serbian and 59 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- let's go back to the page. Can we see the English page as well. I don't think it was translated in full. Do you see the full name, father's name, place of birth, and residence? Let's -- we can collapse the English now. But "not known --" probably underneath notation of "Not known" or whatever, I see entries number 1 and number 2 which are not translated. Could you read out that part for us. We can zoom in a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber would like you to read out something. Perhaps we can clarify it. Is it the name? Is it in that box next to 22?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Muharem Kujovic, the victim, Kujovic. There was his place of residence, and it is also the place where the murder took place, and we have the name of the victim there. Here we have who submitted the report, the name of the victim. We don't see who it was sent to. On the other page we have the measures undertaken and whether any orders were issued by the investigating judge. Perhaps I may explain. It is a large book, a large register, say 70 by 40 centimetres. That is the criminal register. It was kept at Pale as of 1975, and it was used all the way until 2006, when I left the service, and I think they still use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, do you see number 1 and number 2? What I want you to do is read out those two items, number 1 and number 2, in the row of 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could show the -- Lizdek or -- Milo --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranko Makic [phoen], Ivo Andric Street number 16, Pale. These individuals submitted reports to the SJB. In those cases, there was no on-site investigation. These individuals reported crimes to the SJB. There is a date when the report was filed, when it was registered, and here is the aggrieved party, the person whose vehicle was stolen. At that moment it was not known who the perp was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would leave it -- leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the following page in Serbian, and then can we go to page 59 in English. Let's see what happened to Hasim [as interpreted]. 8, Serbian; 59, English. Under 46 in Serbian -- can this be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is it who reported the numbers 46?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: It was the SJB, because its employees carried out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the aggrieved party?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I believe it was Hasim Kujovic from Pale, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the crime? You will see it in the last column.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: A murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked whether you were politically engaged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 13, the name should be Hasna. It's a lady's name, not Hasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- okay. Now I really have to object, and I -- maybe this is something we take outside the -- we discuss outside the presence of the witness, but of all the times not to use a leading interjection and testify as the accused is accustomed to doing, that would have been it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? It's not that you are giving evidence. In order to rectify, you have to ask the witness instead of stating yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to Hasna, it was my intervention on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to the question, I said: Earlier today you were asked on page 35 whether you were politically engaged, and you answered that you were politically engaged in 2012.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: And that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let us establish this: Line 13, page 80. What is the name of the aggrieved party? It has been misrecorded for a number of times. Is it Hasim Kujovic or Hasna Kujovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a -- I think that can be confirmed by the witness, because it is what he said. Yes, Mr. Hrsum. Did you say Hasim or Hasna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hasna. That's what I said, Hasna. I did not utter the name Hasim. Hasim was never a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, does the crime register accurately reflect the name Hasna?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, you confirmed Mr. Tieger's question that you were indeed politically engaged in 2012. I'm asking you this: Were you professionally engaged and politically engaged at the same time, and if you were, when was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: I was never professionally and politically engaged at any time before 2012. At that time, I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now on page 36 there was a reference to discrimination. What was the basis for bringing in individuals and remanding them in custody, primarily those who were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Only crimes before the incident that happened on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Islam religion ever the grounds for remanding people in custody?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 37, it was not fully clarified whether those two or three police officers and crime investigation inspectors left the police or whether they were transferred to another unit. On page 38, you were interrupted when you started your sentence with the words "The procedure to transfer people." Please explain. They left the police or were they transferred?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: If you are referring to the two employees of the crime prevention service and their commander who had been appointed upon agreement, his name was Muslim, Efendic. I will answer this: The procedure for a person to be transferred from one unit to another unit, irrespective of the fact that both units were parts of the Sarajevo SUP, implied the following: First of all, the head of the organisational unit had to agree to hire that person. The head of the organisational unit that that person was leaving also had to be obtained [as interpreted]. All that was confirmed by the secretary of the SUP, and that was what constituted the regular transfer of one person from one unit to another. All those three individuals who were transferred immediately started working in Sarajevo, one in Ilidza, one in Stari Grad, and I believe that Efendic started working in the republican SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the secretary of the city SUP at the time? Was that procedure complied with?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: It was Mico Stanisic, and that procedure was not complied with. It was not complied with at the public security station at Pale either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 6034 is a document that was mentioned. Zdravko Cvoro, the president of the Executive Board, sent some objections to the effect that some Muslims participated in the forcible transfer of some other Muslims. Somebody provided that information to Mr. Cvoro. Did it prove to be correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: You mentioned that Muslims participated in the forcible transfer of Muslims. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Policemen.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Police officers never took part in forceable transfer. They never advocated forcible transfer of Muslims. Police officers were only engaged in providing security. They only took measures in order to protect Muslims in the area. As far as the letter of the president of the Executive Board is concerned, I must say that at the beginning of the war and the course of the war, the local authorities always wanted to place under their control the local police security stations. They wanted to issue them orders as to how they would do their policing work. It was not just the case in Pale. It spilled over to other municipalities as well. They also wanted to place under their control those military units that were set up later. However, no single public security station was under the control of the local authorities. They reported to their superiors in the ministry, i.e., in the MUP, which were the CSBs along the lines of control and ultimately to the minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can P6034 be displayed? Let us see who Mr. Cvoro had in mind when he drafted his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, could you please read the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask those who can follow in English to look at the document off the screen, i.e., could the English be collapsed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the document be shown on the screen for their benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He addresses the War Commission of Pale municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you'd like the witness to read out the document, we need to show the English page to the interpreters. We all have it, so why don't you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I wanted, for all the other participants in the trial to be provided with the off-screen copy of the document. Could you please read the document for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you know the situation. Interpreters do not have access to the English page independently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, maybe I did not say this on time. I didn't ask the witness to read the document aloud. I just wanted him to look at it, and then once he had -- has looked at it, I will have a question to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but is there some reason we're not looking at the document at the same time and have it available in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We did that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for the benefit of the witness so that he could read it. But you have access to English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I do. I just wanted the participants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, earlier today Mr. Tieger suggested to you that the police participated in the forcible transfer of Muslims from Pale contrary to the decision which was passed on the 18th of June, the one that we have seen today. When you look at this document, would you say that it were the police who did that or is it, rather, that Mr. Cvoro is complaining? What is Mr. Cvoro complaining about? Does the document say that the police were involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Either the witness is being asked to simply recite what he sees in the document or he's being asked for an interpretation of this document in a manner that is outside the province of most witnesses, unless they're called as some kind of expert. So I don't -- I mean, in -- for previous questions, Mr. Karadzic has been asking the witness for information that he might have had, and this is straying into an area that's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, you may answer to the question what Mr. Cvoro was complaining about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I'm looking at this document, and I didn't know anything about its existence, Mr. Cvoro is complaining about the arbitrariness, about the lack of organisation, about the forcible transfer of Muslims on the part of the police which caused some problems. However, his ultimate request is for the municipal authorities -- or, rather, my impression is that the municipal authorities managed to exercise control over the police station, and he refers to some other presidents of the Executive Boards that had the same problems. However, the police station acted on their instruction, and they did it in a safe way. Nobody was hurt. Nobody experienced anything bad among those who wanted to move out of their own will -- will. That transfer process did not last only a day or two. It lasted much longer. Some problems arose, and some Muslims were even afraid that they would not be able to move out because the municipal authorities had not set up their commissions on time, so the lists of the population were not compiled, i.e., their immovable properties that they were leaving behind. This is why the process took somewhat longer. And later on -- okay. It lasted a bit longer, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the document once again. Tell us where it is that Mr. Cvoro pinpoints the police as perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, that's why I wanted the witness to have a good look at the document and give us his answer, not as an expert but as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The point you were -- objected to was how you put the question, not the content. Refrain from asking a leading question. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see here that he mentions the police anywhere here. He does not mention the police. The only time he mentions the police is when he says that the police station does not report to them directly. It would probably be better that -- if they had the police station under their authority. I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You as a police officer, what inferences would you make? Who is it that Mr. Cvoro pinpoints as the perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: When it comes to those criminal acts, he pinpoints individuals or -- or, rather, he points to some groups or one may even conclude that he pinpoints at some Muslims who put pressure on each other to move out. He is not very specific in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to continue my objection, and I think the last answer reflects the impropriety of this exercise asking this witness basically to offer some speculations about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger was very express and confronted Mr. Hrsum with the fact that the police participated in unlawful transfer. I'll tell you the exact page. Now, I'm trying to establish who it is that Mr. Cvoro complains? Who does he pinpoint as perpetrators? Let's leave aside the fact that he wants control over the police. Does he pinpoint the police as the main culprits, and if he does, where, in what line? This arises from the Prosecutor's suggestions during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was reading the questions by Mr. Tieger, but I don't think he put the question it was police that wilfully forced the population out. Did you ask such a question, Mr. Tieger? 43, 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the exact language. It is correct that I addressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A role of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that's right, addressed these documents, but I simply recited the language in the document and asked if that didn't reflect the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you referred to P6034 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and lines 20, 21, that said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That document revealed about the role of the police in moving Muslims out. So it's fair enough to ask whether this document pinpointed the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- police but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's a bit of mixing and matching here by -- that's why I was looking at the transcript. I pointed to this document in the context of asking questions about Muslims being forced out and the reflections on that. I turned to D00031 in connection with the complaints of the president of the Assembly and president of the Executive Committee and president of the Crisis Staff about police involvement. So Dr. Karadzic seems to be turning to another document and trying -- I was -- that's why I was looking to see whether there was explicit reference to this document in that connection, but I do know there was a reference to the language of D00031, which is not being addressed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Hrsum. You saw the statement of Sulejman Crncalo who says that on the 3rd of March, 1992, there were beatings in the police. What was the ethnic make-up of the police at the Pale police station on the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: On that date the ethnic make-up was unchanged. It was the same as before, when both Muslims and Serbs -- I don't think we had any Croats perform police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did any of the Muslim policemen confirm that on the 3rd of March someone was beaten up because of their ethnicity or religion?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: There was never such a complaint at the police station, nor did it ever come up, nor was it ever recorded by anyone, nor did anyone ever discuss any such thing. At the entrance to the police station there were two duty officers, and it was always two members of the Serb ethnic group and two Muslims who did that so that this cannot be correct. It was never anything that was confirmed or not confirmed or anything that was acted upon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Hrsum. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have just a couple questions arising in connection with the register, Mr. President, if the Court would permit. You may recall that Mr. Karadzic took the witness's -- took the witness to certain entries and I have a couple of questions about those particular entries. I can make it brief if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hrsum, in paragraph 23 of your statement -- is it 23? That's where you make reference to the criminal report filed in connection with the murder of Muharem Hasna and Ramiz Kujovic. Do I understand, because you reference them together, that those people were killed at the same time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: No, they were not killed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they were killed at different times?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: At different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why is it called an unknown perpetrator for three different murders?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: Because we didn't discover who the perpetrator was. We didn't have into -- we didn't have any information as to who had done this and under what conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says a criminal report was also filed against an unknown perpetrator. Perpetrator singular, report singular. Is that what happened or were there multiple reports?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: There were multiple criminal reports as you can see from the log-book. So these reports were submitted individually, but as the perpetrator was unknown, it implies neither the singular nor the plural. It refers to each perpetrator of each criminal offence, or several perpetrators, but this was the form of words that was normally used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, the date of submission of the report listed in item 46 on page 59 of the English was subsequent to the report by Mr. Micic which we saw earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload D2851. Item 46, page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 8 in Serbian. English, 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If it's taking too much time, I can let the document speak for itself unless it needs to be translated. Okay. It's up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just read the dates of the submitter -- of the submission and the dates of the report. And tell us quickly again what those two dates represent.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV HRSUM
utterances.text: The first date, I don't see it up there, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you -- if you touch it, it -- all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I apologise. The first date is the date when information was received or when the criminal offence was learned of. The second date is the date of submission of the final file to the public prosecutor's office, although the public prosecutor's office was aware based on the log-book of what was going on. Mr. Micic, if it has to do with when he -- I think that his report is dated March 1993, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we clarify this? Can we look at Micic's report, P6092, only to establish the chronology of dates, to see whether Mr. Hrsum spoke correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's in our evidence. Would you like to spend time for that? I think it's in March or May in 1993. You can leave it there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we established that this was after the 20th of May, 1992, then everything is all right, and I don't need to go into it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not in the position to confirm that. Let us see it, then. Could you remind us of the exhibit number, Mr. Tieger, Micic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was either 6092 or 6091. I have them under ERNs at the moment.
